title: Subnetting You Can Actually See

sections.title: One network, four smaller networks
sections.narration: Subnetting has a reputation for ruining a peaceful afternoon. But today we're just splitting one address block into four equal parts. Let's use the bits to explain the boundaries, instead of trying to memorize a giant table.
sections.takeaway: Subnetting divides an existing address block into smaller prefix blocks.

sections.title: IPv4 addresses contain thirty-two bits
sections.narration: An IPv4 address has thirty-two bits, written as four numbers called octets. Each octet holds eight bits. The dots are there to help us read it. They aren't extra bits hiding between the numbers.
sections.takeaway: Dotted decimal is a readable way to write the underlying bits.

sections.title: A prefix marks the shared beginning
sections.narration: Slash twenty-four means the first twenty-four bits are fixed for this block. The final eight can change. Think of a shared building address followed by changing room details: same beginning, different addresses inside the group.
sections.takeaway: The prefix length counts leading network bits, not decimal digits.

sections.title: The mask expresses the boundary
sections.narration: The mask marks fixed network positions with ones and the remaining positions with zeros. For slash twenty-four, that becomes 255.255.255.0. It's a guide telling us which part of the address we're keeping as the network prefix.
sections.takeaway: A contiguous subnet mask and its prefix length describe the same boundary.

sections.title: Find the network with bitwise AND
sections.narration: AND sounds more mysterious than it is. A mask bit of one keeps the address bit; zero clears it. Apply our slash-twenty-four mask to address forty-two, and the network part becomes 192.168.1.0.
sections.takeaway: Masking an address identifies the prefix block that contains it.

sections.title: Count the parent block
sections.narration: Eight changeable bits give two to the power of eight combinations: 256 addresses, from zero through 255 in the last octet. That's the total count. We still need to work out which addresses ordinary hosts can use.
sections.takeaway: Count all addresses before applying ordinary LAN host reservations.

sections.title: Borrow two bits for four subnets
sections.narration: One more fixed prefix bit splits the block into two. Add another, and we get four pieces. We've borrowed two bits, so slash twenty-four becomes slash twenty-six. The scary part was really just dividing twice.
sections.takeaway: Extending a prefix creates smaller blocks within the original block.

sections.title: Build the slash-twenty-six mask
sections.narration: Those two new mask bits are worth 128 and 64. Add them: 192. The remaining six positions are zero, giving mask 255.255.255.192. The decimal number comes straight from the binary positions, not from a lucky guess.
sections.takeaway: Two leading ones in the last octet make the /26 boundary.

sections.title: Six host bits make sixty-four addresses
sections.narration: Now each subnet has six changeable host bits. Two to the power of six gives sixty-four addresses. Four blocks times sixty-four equals our original 256. Nothing disappeared, and we haven't accidentally invented extra addresses.
sections.takeaway: The four /26 blocks exactly cover the original /24.

sections.title: The four binary prefixes
sections.narration: Try the two borrowed bits: zero-zero, zero-one, one-zero, one-one. Clear the host bits, and the network starts become zero, sixty-four, 128, and 192. These are the boundaries we'll use to sort our addresses.
sections.takeaway: Aligned /26 network starts are separated by 64 addresses.

sections.title: Subnet one: zero through sixty-three
sections.narration: Our first block runs from zero through sixty-three. For an ordinary LAN, zero names the network and sixty-three is broadcast. That leaves one through sixty-two for hosts. The first and last addresses have special jobs.
sections.takeaway: Subnet one contains 64 total addresses and 62 ordinary host addresses.

sections.title: Subnet two: sixty-four through 127
sections.narration: The next block starts at sixty-four and ends at 127. Hosts use sixty-five through 126. Notice that broadcast doesn't end in 255 here. The prefix decides the boundary; 255 isn't a universal broadcast password.
sections.takeaway: Network and broadcast roles depend on the prefix, not just the last octet.

sections.title: Subnet three: 128 through 191
sections.narration: Third block: 128 through 191. Keep its subnet bits fixed and let the six host bits change. That gives ordinary host addresses 129 through 190. Same rule again, with a different starting point.
sections.takeaway: Clear host bits while preserving the complete 26-bit network prefix.

sections.title: Subnet four: 192 through 255
sections.narration: The last block runs from 192 through 255, with hosts 193 through 254. Put all four blocks together and we cover the parent exactly once. No missing addresses, no overlap, and nobody assigned the same room twice.
sections.takeaway: Nonoverlapping contiguous ranges verify the subdivision.

sections.title: Locate the host ending in seventy
sections.narration: Where does address seventy belong? Its binary is 01000110. AND that with 11000000, and we get sixty-four. So 192.168.1.70 belongs to 192.168.1.64 slash twenty-six. The mask has sorted it for us.
sections.takeaway: A range check and a mask operation should identify the same subnet.

sections.title: Same prefix or a different subnet?
sections.narration: Seventy and one hundred both belong to the block starting at sixty-four. But 130 belongs to the block starting at 128. Similar-looking addresses aren't enough. Compare their masked prefixes, just like checking the full room information.
sections.takeaway: Compare masked network prefixes, using the relevant mask.

sections.title: Remote destinations use a router
sections.narration: A host usually reaches an address in its own subnet locally. For another subnet, it uses a suitable next-hop router. The boundary changes the forwarding decision. It doesn't mean the devices must be in different physical buildings.
bullets: Remote subnet: use a next-hop router
sections.takeaway: A gateway connects networks that have different prefixes.

sections.title: Choose a prefix for fifty hosts
sections.narration: We need room for fifty hosts. Slash twenty-seven gives thirty usable addresses on an ordinary LAN, so that's too small. Slash twenty-six gives sixty-two. Choose enough space for the class, rather than hoping the extra students won't attend.
sections.takeaway: Choose enough host bits for the requirement and reserved addresses.

sections.title: More prefix bits, fewer addresses
sections.narration: Here's a useful pattern: a longer prefix means a smaller block. Slash twenty-five has 128 total addresses, slash twenty-six has sixty-four, and slash twenty-seven has thirty-two. Every extra fixed bit halves the number of combinations left.
sections.takeaway: Every additional fixed bit halves the number of address combinations.

sections.title: The subtract-two rule has exceptions
sections.narration: Before we turn 'subtract two' into a life rule, here are the exceptions. Suitable slash-thirty-one point-to-point links use both addresses. Slash thirty-two identifies one address. Always check what kind of network we're actually describing.
sections.takeaway: The total-address formula is general; host usability depends on context.

sections.title: A subnet is not a security policy
sections.narration: A subnet is an address and routing boundary, not a security wall. It doesn't encrypt data or block every crossing. Routing rules and access policies decide what can pass between subnets. Different groups don't automatically mean locked doors.
sections.takeaway: A prefix boundary does not replace a security policy.

sections.title: CIDR replaces the classful shortcut
sections.narration: Don't guess the prefix from the first number. Modern classless addressing uses the prefix we're given. Also, our 192.168.1 examples are private addresses. They're useful inside networks, not globally routable addresses for the public Internet.
sections.takeaway: Read the actual prefix instead of guessing an old default class.

sections.title: Check all four answers
sections.narration: Let's check our work like we'd check an exam answer. Starts: zero, sixty-four, 128, 192. Broadcasts: sixty-three, 127, 191, 255. Each block has sixty-four addresses. Check the boundaries before handing out host addresses.
bullets: Each ordinary LAN has 62 host slots
sections.takeaway: Verify alignment, size, boundaries, and coverage before assigning addresses.

sections.title: Move the boundary, solve the puzzle
sections.narration: That's the whole trick: two borrowed bits made four subnets, and six host bits gave sixty-four addresses in each. Once the boundary makes sense, AND and the address ranges stop looking like separate facts to memorize.
sections.takeaway: Subnetting follows directly from fixed prefixes and variable address bits.
